messages.text: I'm a single guy making $1,725 a month. Can I get food stamps?

**You might be able to get food assistance (SNAP).** Your income looks close to the line, so I need a few more details.

**What I found**
- The federal limit for one person is about **$1,729 a month** in income before taxes, starting October 1, 2026. Your $1,725 is just under that.
- Tennessee may now use a higher limit, about 200% of poverty. That would be roughly $2,608 for one person. Reports disagree on whether the change has started, so I can't say for sure which limit applies. Either way, **I'd encourage you to apply.**
- I couldn't open the USDA pages or an official Tennessee page that confirms these numbers. They come from search summaries, so please treat them as approximate. The state agency makes the final call.

**Why your rent and bills matter**
The state subtracts some costs from your income before it works out your benefit. These include a standard amount (about $217), 20% of any wages, and your housing and utility costs. A single person's top benefit is about $306 a month. Lower rent means a smaller benefit, and it could be $0. Higher rent and utility costs can mean more.

**Two questions**
1. Is the $1,725 your pay **before taxes**, and is it from a job? Or is it Social Security, disability, or something else?
2. How much is your rent or mortgage each month? Do you pay separately for heating or cooling?

With those answers I can give you a rough monthly estimate.

**How to apply now**
- Online: [One DHS portal](https://onedhs.tn.gov). This is the Tennessee Department of Human Services' application site.
- Phone: 1-833-772-8347 (TTY 711)
- Free local help: call 211.
- Source I opened: [Tennessee Department of Human Services SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html)

Please report your income and household accurately on the application. That protects you, because overpayments have to be paid back.

I'm not totally sure what counts as income for this. It's my paycheck from my job, about $1,725 a month. I don't know if that's before or after taxes, though. I think it's what gets deposited, so maybe after taxes? My rent is $500 a month and utilities are included, so no separate heating or cooling bills. I don't have any other income or bills I'm aware of. I've got about $200 in savings. Is that enough info to get a rough idea?

Yes, that's enough for a rough idea. **The estimate is that your benefit would be small, possibly $0.** You can still apply, and the state makes the final decision.

**First, check your pay stub.** SNAP counts income *before* taxes. A deposit is usually after taxes, so your pay before taxes is probably higher than $1,725. The stub shows it as "gross pay."

**Rough math if $1,725 is before taxes** (these numbers are from search summaries, because I couldn't open the USDA pages):
- Start with $1,725.
- Subtract 20% for working (about $345). That leaves about $1,380.
- Subtract the standard amount (about $217). That leaves about $1,163.
- Your $500 rent is less than half of that, so you get no extra housing deduction.
- SNAP expects you to spend about 30% of that $1,163 on food, which is about $349. The top benefit for one person is about $306.
- That makes your estimate **about $0**. Some single people get a $25 minimum, but I'm not sure that applies here.

**If $1,725 is after taxes:** Your pay before taxes is higher, maybe $1,950 to $2,050. That is over the federal 130% limit of about $1,729. Tennessee may use a higher limit (about 200%, or $2,608), but reports disagree on whether it has started. So the result is *possibly*, and the benefit would still likely be $0 or very small.

**Other notes**
- Your $200 in savings is not a problem.
- Adults without children can have work rules. Since you work, you likely meet them, but a caseworker will confirm.

**Next steps**
- Apply at the [One DHS portal](https://onedhs.tn.gov), or call 1-833-772-8347 (TTY 711).
- Call 211 for free local help.
- Applying costs nothing, and a caseworker will use your real pay stub.
- Source I opened: [Tennessee Department of Human Services SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html)

Do you want me to check whether you might qualify for TennCare (Tennessee's health coverage)? If so, tell me your age and whether you have health insurance now.
Yeah, go ahead and check TennCare. I'm 38 and I don't have health insurance right now. My job doesn't offer it, and I can't afford to buy it on my own.

**TennCare looks unlikely for you, but you can still apply.** Tennessee hasn't expanded Medicaid. Search results consistently say adults without children, who aren't pregnant, disabled, or 65 or older, generally can't get TennCare, whatever their income.

I couldn't open the official TennCare pages, so this comes from search summaries. They were mostly third-party sites. I'm not linking them as sources because I haven't confirmed what they say. Only TennCare can tell you for sure.

**TennCare could still apply if:**
- You have a disability, or get SSI (Supplemental Security Income).
- You're caring for a child under 19 in your home.
- You were in foster care and are under 26. (You're 38, so this wouldn't apply.)

Tell me if any of those fit. I can look further.

**Better options for you right now**
1. **The Health Insurance Marketplace.** Your income is in the range where you can usually get help paying for a plan. The extra help that started in 2021 ended after 2025, so premiums are higher than before. Even so, the help may still make a plan cheaper.
   - Website: HealthCare.gov
   - The phone number I remember is 1-800-318-2596, but I couldn't confirm it today.
2. **Losing a job's coverage isn't your situation.** You don't have a special enrollment reason I can see, so open enrollment (usually November through mid-January) is your main window. It starts soon.
3. **Low-cost clinics.** Community health centers charge based on income. Call 211 to find one near you.

**To apply for TennCare anyway:** Use the One DHS portal at [onedhs.tn.gov](https://onedhs.tn.gov). This is the same site as for food assistance, and I opened that page earlier. TennCare will review your application and tell you if there's a way you qualify. For TennCare questions, call 211 or the TennCare line, which I believe is 1-855-259-0701 but couldn't verify.

Do you have a disability, or does anyone under 19 live with you? Those two answers could change this result.
No, I'm not disabled and I don't get SSI. Nobody under 19 lives with me. I live alone.

Thanks. With those answers, **TennCare looks unlikely for you**. I couldn't open the official TennCare pages, so this comes from search summaries. Only TennCare can decide. If your situation changes, for example a disability, a child moving in, or turning 65, check again, because those can change the result.

**What I'd do now**
1. **Look at the Health Insurance Marketplace.** Your income is in the range where you can usually get help paying for a plan.
   - Website: HealthCare.gov
   - Open enrollment usually starts November 1, so it's close.
   - Premiums are higher this year than before, because the extra help ended after 2025. Compare plans anyway, because the help can still lower your cost a lot.
   - The Marketplace asks for your income before taxes. Check your pay stub for that number.
2. **Find a low-cost clinic.** Community health centers charge based on income, even without insurance. Call 211 for one near you.
3. **Apply for food assistance (SNAP).** It's still worth a try. Use the [One DHS portal](https://onedhs.tn.gov) or call 1-833-772-8347 (TTY 711). Your income is near the limit, so the benefit may be small or $0, as we talked about. I opened the [Tennessee Department of Human Services SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html) for that.

You can also apply for TennCare on that same portal if you want a formal answer. It costs nothing.

If you'd like, I can look up what Marketplace plans might cost for someone with your income.
Okay, got it. Is there anything else I should know before I apply for food stamps? Like do I need to bring my pay stub or can I just do it online?

You can do it all online. You don't have to go to an office.

**What I confirmed:** On the [Tennessee Department of Human Services SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html), you can apply on the One DHS portal ([onedhs.tn.gov](https://onedhs.tn.gov)) any time of day. You can also upload documents there and report changes. If you'd rather talk to someone, call 1-833-772-8347 (TTY 711).

**What to have ready**
- **Recent pay stubs.** Yes, bring or upload them. They show your pay *before taxes*, which answers your question from earlier. Use that number on the application, not the deposit amount.
- **Proof of rent.** A lease or a rent receipt works. Also have something showing utilities are included, if you have it.
- **ID.** Have a photo ID or similar.

I'm going from general knowledge on these documents. The page I opened doesn't list them, so the caseworker will tell you exactly what they need.

**Other things to know**
- **Apply as soon as you can.** Benefits can start from the date they receive your application, even if the paperwork takes a while. I couldn't confirm this today, so ask when you apply.
- **Expect an interview.** Programs like this usually do one, often by phone. Watch for calls or mail from the state and answer them. Missing it can delay or end your application.
- **Report everything accurately.** That means your pay, rent, and who lives with you. If you report something wrong, even by accident, you may have to pay back benefits.
- **If you're turned down, you can ask for a review.** The notice will explain how.
- **Free help:** Call 211.

The state makes the final decision. I can't promise an outcome. Your income is close to the limit, so applying is the only way to find out for sure.

The FY 2027 SNAP adjustments took effect October 1, 2026, and the USDA memo is the primary source. For the 48 states and D.C., the key figures are:

- **Shelter cap:** The maximum excess shelter deduction rises to $769 in the 48 states and D.C. The shelter cap value will increase to $769 for the 48 States and D.C.
- **Standard deduction:** For households of one to three, it is $217. The FY 2027 schedule also sets $229 for four, $268 for five, and $308 for six or more (For FY 2027 in the 48 states and D.C. the SNAP standard deduction is $217 for households of one to three, $229 for four, $268 for five and $308 for six or more.).
- **Maximum allotment:** A family of four gets up to $1,023. The maximum allotment for a family of four in the 48 States and D.C., will be $1,023. Other sources list a single person at $306 and a household of five at $1,217 (1 person: $306 ... 5 people: $1,217).
- **Cap for large households:** For FY 2027, this caps the maximum allotment for households with 18 or more persons at $3,887 in the 48 States and the District of Columbia.
- **Minimum benefit:** The minimum benefit for the 48 States and D.C. will increase to $25.

Other territories and states differ. Hawaii's four-person maximum falls to $1,655, and the U.S. Virgin Islands' shelter deduction is $606 (The maximum in the Virgin Islands will be $606).

Source conflict: one Cronista article gives the shelter deduction as $789, up from $744 (The maximum excess shelter deduction increases from $744 to $789 in the 48 states and D.C.). The USDA memo and several other outlets say $769, so the $789 figure appears to be an error. The USDA memo should be treated as authoritative.

Adults without children generally cannot get TennCare in 2026, regardless of income. Tennessee has not expanded Medicaid, so the main exceptions are based on disability, age, pregnancy, or a dependent.

- **Who can qualify:** One source lists pregnant women, people 65 or older, blind or disabled people, and former foster youth under 26. Adults without dependent children can't qualify unless they are pregnant, 65 or older, blind, disabled, or a former foster youth under 26.
- **Disability and aged categories:** One source gives an income limit of up to $994 a month and resources up to $2,000 for these groups. Another notes that SSI recipients automatically qualify for TennCare, with no separate application needed.
- **Basic requirements:** You must live in Tennessee, be a U.S. citizen or have an eligible immigration status, and give a Social Security number.
- **Ways to apply:** There's no open enrollment period for Medicaid.
- **Future change:** One source says a federal work rule arrives in 2027, but it reaches only some waiver parents. A separate opinion-style article discusses 2026 work-requirement debates, but it is not a source for current rules.

For childless adults who don't qualify, the guides point to ACA Marketplace coverage. Several sources say non-disabled adults without dependent children are generally not eligible for Medicaid regardless of income.

Caveats: Most of these results are from third-party benefit websites, not official state pages. Their income figures conflict. For example, one site says pregnant women qualify up to 250% FPL, while another says pregnant women qualify up to 250% FPL, and a third gives $2,596 (200% FPL). Verify current limits at tn.gov/tenncare before relying on them.

The search turned up consistent reporting that the enhanced credits lapsed for 2026, with the standard subsidy schedule now in effect for single adults in Tennessee.

- **Expiration:** One source says the enhanced credit expired December 31, 2025 and was not extended by OBBBA. Another notes that the enhanced credits are expiring on Dec. 31, 2025 and will not be renewed. Earlier coverage from September 2025 described Congress as still debating an extension, so those pieces predate the outcome.
- **400% cliff:** For 2026, the pre-2021 schedule applies. One source describes a hard cliff at 400% of the Federal Poverty Level — no premium tax credit at all above it, with required contributions near 9.96% of income just below that line. That source's table is illustrative and uses a single-person income of $62,600 at 400% FPL.
- **100% to 400% range:** A Tennessee agent presentation says traditional APTC's (100-400% FPL) will remain in place for 2026 plans. Members who lose the enhanced credits will see an increase in their monthly premiums.
- **Premium impact:** Tennessee's year-over-year increase in marketplace premiums is partly attributed to the expiration. One BCBST figure says its Marketplace rates will increase an average 42% in 2026, and that same release lists the end of the enhanced credits among several causes.
- **Coverage gap:** Tennessee has not expanded Medicaid, so residents below 100% FPL can fall into the "coverage gap", where they are too poor for marketplace subsidies but above the state's Medicaid limit for adults without children.
- **Enrollment:** Tennessee uses the federally-facilitated marketplace — shop for plans and enroll through HealthCare.gov.

I did not find a source confirming the final congressional status after the lapse, and the premium figures are from insurer and advocacy sources. The 400% cliff figure comes from a single secondary source, so check HealthCare.gov or IRS guidance before relying on it.
